l: Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models, I.
s: This unit examines the use of large language models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for Quranic studies, especially the retrieval of reliable and contextually relevant information. It compares 13 open-source LLMs using a dataset about the 114 surahs of the Qur’an rather than the Qur’an text itself. The study evaluates context relevance, response faithfulness, and answer relevance through human evaluation, with the goal of reducing hallucination and improving transparency through citations. It also considers the trade-offs among model size, performance, and computational efficiency in religious and culturally sensitive applications.

l: natural language processing, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models, I.
s: Natural language processing has been transformed by the development of large language models, which support tasks such as summarization, translation, domain-specific question answering, and annotation. l: large language models, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models, I.
s: Large language models can perform a wide range of activities, including summarization, translation, domain-specific question answering, and annotation. The unit examines their use in Quranic studies and compares 13 open-source models in terms of accuracy, faithfulness, performance, and efficiency. Their use in religious or culturally sensitive settings raises concerns about accuracy, contextual relevance, authenticity, distortion, and hallucination.

l: Qur’anic studies, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models, I.
s: Quranic studies is presented as a domain in which natural language processing and large language models can support question answering and knowledge retrieval. l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models, I.
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation integrates large language model semantics with a vector database to retrieve relevant information from descriptive datasets. In this study, it is used to reduce hallucination, improve response relevance, ground answers in authoritative and contextually appropriate sources, and provide citations that support traceability and transparency.

l: Qur’an, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models, I.

s: Quranic knowledge retrieval is the focus of the study’s application of the Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework. s: This research study benchmarks 13 open-source large language models within a Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework for Quranic studies. l: hallucinations, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models, I.
s: Hallucination is identified as a major challenge in using large language models for religious and culturally sensitive topics. The study uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation and source citations to reduce the likelihood that responses contain unsubstantiated or irrelevant information.

l: Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models, Investigating Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Quranic Studies: A Study of 13 Open-Source Large Language Models, II.

Human evaluators score the responses on a five-point Likert scale, while Fleiss’ Kappa measures Inter-Evaluator Agreement. The study compares Llama, Gemma, QwQ, and Phi models using specified hardware and software resources.

l: VisDoM: Multi-Document QA with Visually Rich Elements Using Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: This unit is a paper in Volume 1 of the Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies, held April 29–May 4, 2025. Titled “VisDoM: Multi-Document QA with Visually Rich Elements Using Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation,” it is by Manan Suri, Puneet Mathur, Franck Dernoncourt, Kanika Gowswami, Ryan A. Rossi, and Dinesh Manocha, affiliated with the University of Maryland, College Park, Adobe Research, and IGDTUW. The paper addresses question answering over multi-page PDF documents whose relevant evidence may be spread across documents and include text, tables, charts, and slides. It first positions Retrieval Augmented Generation against text-centric and single-document benchmarks, then introduces VisDoMBench, a multi-document multimodal benchmark built from PaperTab, FeTaTab, SciGraphQA, SPIQA, and SlideVQA. VisDoMBench contains 2,271 queries across 1,277 documents and uses sourcing, sampling, de-duplication, document augmentation, and query augmentation to retain grounded evidence. The paper then presents VisDoMRAG, which runs parallel textual and visual retrieval pipelines: the textual pipeline uses OCR-based text, while the visual pipeline retrieves pages with graphical information. Its modality fusion uses evidence curation, chain-of-thought reasoning, and consistency analysis to reconcile the two pipelines. Experiments compare text retrieval methods including BM25, MPNet, MiniLM, and BGE-1.5; visual retrieval methods ColPali and ColQwen2; and end-to-end Long Context, TextualRAG, VisualRAG, and VisDoMRAG systems using Qwen2-VL, Gemini-1.5-Flash, and ChatGPT-4o. ColQwen2 performs best among retrieval baselines, and VisDoMRAG generally exceeds the other QA approaches by 12–20%, with visual RAG particularly useful on visually rich data. Ablations favor late fusion and structured prompting. The paper concludes that the benchmark and system improve multimodal multi-document QA, while noting dependence on text extraction and parsing, three LLM calls per query, hallucination and safety risks, and difficulty isolating visual performance when document context contributes to answers. Future work targets end-to-end trained models and low-resource settings.

l: VisDoMBench, VisDoM: Multi-Document QA with Visually Rich Elements Using Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: VisDoMBench is a comprehensive, first-of-its-kind multi-document, multimodal document question-answering benchmark and QA dataset for visually rich content. It evaluates systems that must answer questions across document sets containing text, tables, charts, and presentation slides, requiring both textual and visual comprehension. The benchmark contains 2,271 queries and 1,277 documents, spans multiple domains, includes diverse question types and annotated grounded evidence, and represents each data point as a question, a document set, and a ground-truth answer. It combines PaperTab, FeTaTab, SciGraphQA, SPIQA, and SlideVQA. Its construction uses publicly accessible source documents, removes overlap between PaperTab and SPIQA, deduplicates QA pairs and similar questions across collections, adds distracting documents to simulate realistic multi-document settings, and augments queries with specific question variations generated with GPT-4o. VisDoMBench provides a more comprehensive multi-domain evaluation framework for multimodal retrieval and end-to-end QA. In experiments, it benchmarks large language models and compares retrieval and end-to-end question answering across its component datasets. Retrieval is evaluated with ANLCS and document-retrieval accuracy, while end-to-end results use Word Overlap F1 and compare multiple RAG and long-context approaches. It is introduced and concluded as a benchmark for multi-document systems incorporating rich visual elements.

l: VisDoMRAG, VisDoM: Multi-Document QA with Visually Rich Elements Using Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: VisDoMRAG is a proposed multimodal retrieval-augmented generation system and approach for multi-document, visually rich document question answering. Its central design is to run visual RAG and textual RAG concurrently rather than relying on only one modality or a long context. First, Evidence-driven Parallel Unimodal RAG retrieves relevant pages and chunks from a multi-document source through parallel visual and textual pipelines. Within each modality, it performs evidence curation and chain-of-thought reasoning to generate modality-specific answers. Second, Modality Fusion ensembles these outputs: at inference time, a consistency-constrained modality-fusion mechanism evaluates reasoning-chain consistency, aligns reasoning across modalities, and produces the final answer. This fusion is intended to improve answer verifiability through implicit context attribution while constraining the context processed by the LLM, helping maintain performance as page counts rise. Across evaluated datasets and LLM settings, VisDoMRAG outperforms Visual RAG, Textual RAG, and Long Context baselines; reported end-to-end improvements are 12%–20%, while gains in the results range from 0.24% to 52.16%. It achieves the highest average score for each listed LLM and an overall average of 50.01 with ChatGPT-4o; prompt ablation reduces the average to 45.98. The work focuses on multimodal multi-document RAG and plans to extend to end-to-end trained models for reasoning, especially in low-resource settings.

l: HYBGRAG: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Textual and Relational Knowledge Bases
s: HYBGRAG: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Textual and Relational Knowledge Bases is a paper by Meng-Chieh Lee, Qi Zhu, Costas Mavromatis, Zhen Han, Soji Adeshina, Vassilis N. Ioannidis, Huzefa Rangwala, and Christos Faloutsos of Carnegie Mellon University and Amazon, published in the Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics. It addresses hybrid question answering over semi-structured knowledge bases that combine knowledge graphs with documents attached to entities. The paper argues that conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation emphasizes text, while Graph RAG emphasizes relational structure, so either can miss questions requiring both sources. The paper identifies two central problems: useful information from textual and relational retrievers is largely non-overlapping, and initial retrieval often requires correction. It proposes HYBGRAG, an agentic framework with a retriever bank and a critic module. The bank includes text and hybrid retrieval modules; a router selects a module and retrieves top-K references. A validator assesses the results, and a commenter supplies corrective feedback when entity extraction, relation extraction, or routing is wrong. Through iterations, the router revises its retrieval choice, topic entities, and relations until the validator accepts the references. Experiments cover STARK-MAG, STARK-PRIME, and CRAG. HYBGRAG reports the best retrieval results on both STARK datasets and the best CRAG results among the compared graph, text, hybrid, and self-reflective baselines. On STARK, it achieves a 51% average relative Hit@1 improvement, including 47% on STARK-MAG and 55% on STARK-PRIME. The paper reports that corrective feedback raises subgraph hit rate from 0.6769 after one iteration to 0.9231 after two. Ablations attribute gains to the critic, iterative reflection, validation context, commenter, and multi-agent design; interpretability examples show switches from failed text retrieval to refined hybrid retrieval. The appendices detail benchmarks, prompts, infrastructure, implementation, API and token use, and additional ablations. The paper closes by noting limitations: simple retrieval modules, limited domain-adaptation advantage, random in-context examples, and weaker performance on STARK-PRIME than STARK-MAG. It suggests alternative rankers, PPR-based retrieval, and relevance-based experience selection as future directions.

l: HYBGRAG, HYBGRAG: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Textual and Relational Knowledge Bases
s: HYBGRAG: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Textual and Relational Knowledge Bases is a research paper and proposed retrieval-augmented generation approach for hybrid question answering in semi-structured knowledge bases. It is built around a retriever bank and a critic module. A chat LLM router selects retrieval, using a Text Retrieval Module when hybrid retrieval is not selected and a hybrid retrieval module when it is. The retriever bank handles textual, relational, and hybrid questions, while iterative self-reflection uses validator and commentor feedback to correct question routing, retrieval-module selection, and extracted entities and relations. This creates an interpretable refinement path, similar to CoT, that justifies its decisions. The method begins by routing a question and retrieving information, then validates the result and receives corrective feedback when needed. It can revise its route over additional iterations; in a STARK-Prime example, it starts with text retrieval and switches to hybrid retrieval after rejection of a document. Reported examples show it adding needed entities and removing unsuitable entities or relations. It performs best among evaluated ablations when all design choices are used and approaches oracle performance. HYBGRAG is evaluated for retrieval on STARK and end-to-end RAG on CRAG. It is reported to surpass baselines on hybrid question answering, including Think-on-Graph, AVATAR, and QAGNN on both STARK datasets, and to outperform CoT, text-only and graph-only RAG, concatenated text-and-graph RAG, ReAct, and Corrective RAG on CRAG. It reports a 51% average relative Hit@1 improvement on STARK, with at most 14 API calls and no training, plus stated STARK-MAG and STARK-PRIME retrieval results. On CRAG, it adapts its modules so text retrieval uses web search and a VSS ranker and hybrid retrieval is replaced by graph retrieval. Limitations include use of simple retrieval modules, no significant domain-adaptation advantage, random experience selection for ICL, and worse performance on STARK-Prime than STARK-MAG.

Its documents are interconnected by relations and provide textual information alongside graph information. SKB serves as the knowledge source for hybrid question answering, where questions may require both relational and textual evidence. HYBGRAG operates over SKB by retrieving references from both the graph and documents for hybrid retrieval, or from documents alone for text retrieval, distinguishing this setting from prior Graph RAG approaches.

It retrieves textual documents to assist large language models in question answering, giving them access to unstructured document databases so they can address unknown facts and Open-Domain Question Answering. Its central limitation is that its text-focused retrieval overlooks interconnections among documents, so it does not meet relational hybrid questions. It is evaluated end to end on CRAG, where HYBGRAG reports higher combined scores than listed text-only, graph-only, text-and-graph, corrective, and self-reflective alternatives.

It centers on relational information or relationships between documents, but existing methods may overlook textual aspects. Its development spans KBQA, which leverages LLM capability; ODQA, which builds document relationships to improve retrieval; and HQA, which answers questions with a given subgraph. Earlier GRAG methods are not easily generalized to HQA in SKB.

They can also be prompted to identify a hybrid question’s relational aspect, topic entities, and useful relations for knowledge-graph subgraph extraction, though refinement may be needed when textual and relational aspects are not distinguished. They support KBQA, planning, and self-reflection; as critics, pre-trained models may give suboptimal, overly implicit feedback without external tools, fine-tuning labels, and careful design. l: HQA, HYBGRAG: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Textual and Relational Knowledge Bases
s: HQA, or hybrid question answering, is a question answering task over a semi-structured knowledge base. It answers hybrid questions by retrieving documents associated with entities that meet both relational and textual requirements. It is the central task addressed by HYBGRAG and studied in STARK. Existing ODQA, KBQA, RAG, Graph RAG, and self-reflective LLM approaches may struggle because they lack suitable retrieval tools or guidance for refining retrieval. HYBGRAG addresses HQA’s textual, relational, and hybrid questions through a retriever bank and critic module, and is reported to outperform existing RAG and GRAG methods.

It includes STARK-MAG and STARK-PRIME, whose test sets contain 2,665 and 2,801 questions. Evaluation uses Hit@1, Hit@5, Recall@20, and mean reciprocal rank. It provides training examples and default entity and relation types; HYBGRAG extracts egographs with radius no more than two and performs four self-reflection iterations. Same-name entities are resolved through an answer-containing one-hop neighborhood. HYBGRAG reports a 51% average relative Hit@1 improvement, including 47% on STARK-MAG and 55% on STARK-PRIME.

l: self-reflection, HYBGRAG: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Textual and Relational Knowledge Bases
s: Self-reflection is a model or agent capability for retrieval, generation, critique, and problem solving. It matters because it corrects incorrect first attempts by iteratively optimizing outputs or question routing from critic feedback, improving retrieval accuracy, interpretability, and HYBGRAG retrieval performance. In HYBGRAG, gains are strongest from one to two iterations, while later iterations yield diminishing improvements. Critics may use pre-trained LLMs, external tools, or fine-tuned LLMs, but poorly designed pre-trained-LLM critics can evaluate suboptimally and give overly implicit feedback. Existing approaches do not generalize to HQA without suitable retrieval tools and retrieval-refinement guidance.

It distinguishes textual topics from relations and selects text or hybrid retrieval. In STARK-Prime, HYBGRAG refines routing through self-reflection and validation feedback, changing text retrieval to hybrid retrieval when needed.

l: critic module, HYBGRAG: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Textual and Relational Knowledge Bases
s: The critic module evaluates retrieved references and the router’s decisions to improve question routing. It contains an LLM validator and an LLM commenter: the validator checks retrieved results, while the commenter provides feedback on incorrect or missing entities and relations. It can identify whether a phrase is a textual aspect rather than a topic entity by comparing ego-graph intersections. Its feedback helps HYBGRAG refine routing and outperform hybrid retrieval alone. Ablation variants alter validators, commenters, and oracles; the full design performs best.

l: STARK-PRIME, HYBGRAG: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Textual and Relational Knowledge Bases
s: STARK-PRIME is a STARK benchmark variant and Hybrid Question Answering STARK dataset for retrieval evaluation. It evaluates HYBGRAG, which reports 55% relative Hit@1 improvement over the second-best baseline and Hit@1 0.2856, Hit@5 0.4138, Recall@20 0.4358, and MRR 0.3449. It then provides examples of question-routing refinement and critic-feedback entity and relation extraction under context, in-context learning, and oracle settings.

l: Think-on-Graph, HYBGRAG: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Textual and Relational Knowledge Bases
s: Think-on-Graph is a graph retrieval baseline implemented with provided code and Claude 3 Sonnet. Because full experiments exceed a week in latency and cost, it is tested on 10% of questions, reporting lower retrieval scores than HYBGRAG on both STARK datasets.

l: AVATAR, HYBGRAG: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Textual and Relational Knowledge Bases
s: AVATAR is a recent LLM agent based on Claude 3 Opus that iteratively optimizes prompts through contrastive reasoning. It requires at least 500 API calls during training, serves as a self-reflective STARK baseline, and is strongest before hybrid retrieval and HYBGRAG, though first attempts may fail.

l: John Smith, HYBGRAG: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Textual and Relational Knowledge Bases
s: John Smith is a person in an example hybrid question, identified as author of nanofluid heat transfer papers and representing its relational aspect.
